rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
θ − θ0 = (θ1 − θ0) e^(−Kt/mc)
Half-excess time = (mc/K) ln 2

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: The temperature does not fall linearly with time.  ·  The body does not overshoot θ0 in this solution.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: The derivation assumes K and c stay constant.  ·  A change of state would add a latent-heat term the separation did not include.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Start from −mc dθ/dt = K (θ − θ0), with K and θ0 constant. This is the rate form of Newton's law of cooling.  ·  Separate the variables: dθ / (θ − θ0) = −(K/mc) dt. Every temperature term is on the left and time is on the right.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: θ1 is the initial temperature, not the surroundings.  ·  The exponent is negative for a hot body, so the excess shrinks.

rows.label: Derivation

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Integrate from the initial temperature θ1 at t = 0 to the temperature θ at time t. The left side becomes the natural log of the ratio of the excesses.  ·  The result is ln[(θ − θ0)/(θ1 − θ0)] = −(K/mc) t. Exponentiating both sides gives θ − θ0 = (θ1 − θ0) e^(−Kt/mc).  ·  The excess temperature therefore falls exponentially. It becomes half in a fixed time that depends on mc/K, and it is never exactly zero at a finite time.
